analysis.one_liner: Makes patents harder to challenge and easier to enforce, while cracking down on scam patent demand letters.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2019 by three Democrats and three Republicans, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it much harder to knock out a patent once it is issued. It would require challengers at the Patent Office to meet a stricter proof standard, limit who can even file a challenge, and block repeat challenges, while making it easier for patent owners to get court orders shutting competitors down. It also ends the practice of diverting Patent Office fees to the general treasury, gives university researchers cheaper patent fees, adds help for small businesses, and makes fraudulent patent demand letters a federal trade violation enforceable by the FTC and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Patent owners, above all brand-name drug makers and firms whose business is licensing or asserting patents. Patents that the Patent Office currently strikes down in its administrative review process would survive, and winning an infringement suit would again usually mean a court order blocking the competitor, which increases the leverage to extract settlements. University researchers and small inventors would get cheaper fees and some procedural help.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Brand-name drug makers and patent owners

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Patent Office to presume an issued patent claim valid and to strike it down only on clear and convincing evidence, a much stricter standard than the office currently applies in inter partes and post-grant reviews.

Bars most companies from filing a patent review unless they have actually been sued or charged with infringement, restricts repeat challenges to the same patent, and blocks reviews of claims a court has already ruled on.

Creates a presumption that further infringement causes irreparable harm, making it easier for a patent owner to win an injunction shutting a competitor's product down after winning an infringement case.
Ends the diversion of Patent Office user fees to the general treasury, letting the office keep and spend what it collects.

Makes bad-faith patent demand letters — demanding money without identifying the patent, the allegedly infringing product, or the real party behind the letter — an unfair trade practice enforced by the FTC and state attorneys general, with penalties up to $5 million per series of violations.
Extends discounted micro-entity patent fees to university researchers and directs courts to develop expedited procedures for small businesses and individuals accused of infringement.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, especially patients who buy brand-name drugs: weaker invalidation tools keep patents, and therefore monopoly pricing, in place longer. Product companies — phones, software, connected devices — would face easier court orders against their products and higher settlement costs when accused of infringement.

drawbacks.text: Raising the bar for invalidating patents would preserve more weak or already-invalidated patents, including on brand-name drugs, delaying generic competition and keeping prices higher for consumers.

Restoring an automatic presumption in favor of injunctions could pull products off the market on the strength of a patent a challenger never got a fair chance to invalidate, and the new standing limits would bar potential competitors from cleaning up bad patents before they are used against them.
The title cracking down on fraudulent demand letters preempts some state laws on the subject, replacing them with a federal regime that caps related penalties at $5 million.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The demand-letter title is a genuine consumer and small-business protection, and keeping Patent Office fees is defensible on its own terms. But the bill's core is a large one-way transfer of leverage to patent owners: stricter proof standards, fewer challengers, and easier injunctions, whose costs would show up mostly in higher drug prices and costlier patent disputes. An honest supporter would have to concede the bill trades a modest anti-scam win for a much bigger strengthening of patent monopolies.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 10, 2019, with a bipartisan group of six senators: sponsor Chris Coons and cosponsors Dick Durbin, Mazie Hirono, Tom Cotton, John Kennedy, and Kevin Cramer.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day.
No further action was ever taken on the bill — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on the Patent Office's review process to defeat patents asserted against them — large technology firms and generic drug makers — keep that cheaper challenge route, and consumers are spared the higher drug prices the bill's patent-strengthening provisions would have supported.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big tech and generic drug makers

sides.party_line_note: The six sponsoring senators split evenly — three Democrats (Coons, Durbin, Hirono) and three Republicans (Cotton, Kennedy, Cramer) — and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a party-line vote.

industries.note: Weaker invalidation tools and easier injunctions would let pharmaceutical patents survive challenges longer, extending the monopoly pricing period before generics arrive. Consumers pay the difference at the pharmacy.

Higher proof standards, new standing limits, and an automatic presumption favoring injunctions would sharply increase settlement leverage over companies accused of infringement. The bill's demand-letter title is the exception, curbing bad-faith shakedown letters.
Generic makers depend on knocking out invalid brand-name patents to enter the market; the bill would make those challenges slower, costlier, and less likely to succeed.
These firms are the heaviest users of Patent Office reviews and would face presumptive injunctions and import blocks that threaten entire product lines over contested patents.

University researchers would get discounted micro-entity fees and small businesses would get expedited court procedures and a Small Business Administration study. These gains ride on a bill whose overall effect is to strengthen patent holders generally.
